summary:
Tonga's Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity between men and between women, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years; the 2010 US State Department human rights report described enforcement of the sodomy provision as rare.

The same statute contains an offence aimed squarely at gender expression: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. Unlike the sodomy provision this turns on visible presentation rather than private conduct, so it bears directly on how a trans visitor may appear and speak in public spaces.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's documents will therefore carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic mechanism to alter it, and nothing in the source material indicates that foreign gender-marker changes are recognised or accepted for any domestic purpose.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or in the provision of goods and services. The Judicial Code of Conduct 2010 requires judges to be aware of diversity including sexual orientation and prohibits bias on irrelevant grounds, but it binds judges only, not employers, service providers or police.

Tonga does not recognise same-sex relationships or unions in any form. No partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights appear anywhere in the sourced material, so a visitor's accompanying partner has no recognised standing with hospitals, authorities or immigration.

Violence risk is documented. LGBTQ activist Polikalepo Kefu was murdered near his home at Muʻa in 2021, and LGBTQ people in Tonga are described as facing a climate of fear, discrimination and homophobia attributed to conservative social values, colonial-era laws, and rising fundamentalism and religious fanaticism that has increased hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleitis.

Tonga, with Kiribati, is the only Polynesian country that has not signed or expressed support for the 2011 UN joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Community infrastructure is thin. The country's LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter on Tongatapu was seriously damaged by Cyclone Gita in February 2018, with winds over 120 mph tearing off part of the roof and damaging bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans; the sources do not record its subsequent repair or replacement.

Public trans visibility nonetheless exists alongside the legal position: a trans pageant was documented in international press coverage in August 2024, evidence that a locally recognised gender-nonconforming identity has a visible cultural presence even without legal protection.
tangentialFactors:
The 2010 US State Department human rights report listed domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption as the country's most prevalent human rights problems, and recorded no government abuses of LGBTQ persons. That finding is fifteen years old and speaks to the state rather than to community-level risk.

Tonga's legal regime is an outlier within Polynesia: neighbouring jurisdictions in the subregion have moved toward decriminalisation or recognition, while Tonga and Kiribati remain the only Polynesian states without support for the 2011 UN joint statement.

The 2024 pageant coverage indicates that visible trans life continues in Tonga despite the absence of legal recognition or anti-discrimination protection, so the practical picture is one of tolerated cultural presence combined with an unenforced but extant criminal statute and no legal remedies.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory remedy for discrimination in employment, housing or the provision of goods and services on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only equality-adjacent instrument on the books is the Judicial Code of Conduct 2010, which constrains judicial conduct alone.

Fakaleitis, a locally recognised gender-nonconforming identity, holds cultural visibility, and LGBTI community organisation has centred on a drop-in centre and shelter on Tongatapu that was badly damaged by Cyclone Gita in 2018. No sourced material confirms the facility's current operating status.

Same-sex couples have no route to partnership, marriage or legal recognition, and no next-of-kin standing is conferred on partners, which affects hospital visitation, inheritance and custody for resident couples as well as visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement data for the trans-expression provision is absent. The inventory records that the sodomy provision has not been enforced in recent years but gives no case history, arrest data or judicial application for the public-solicitation offence targeting gender presentation, so its real-world use remains unresolved.

The UK Foreign Office travel advice for Tonga produced no usable finding in the source inventory; nothing is recorded there about entry screening, document inspection or border questioning that could out a trans visitor.

No sourced material addresses detention conditions for trans or gender-nonconforming detainees, police treatment of gender-nonconforming persons, or access to gender-affirming healthcare. These gaps are unverified rather than confirmed as absent.

The current operational status of the Tonga LGBTI drop-in centre and shelter after the 2018 cyclone damage is not sourced.
